chapter.v:
King Solomon
loved many foreign women. Besides Pharaoh's daughter, there were women from the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Sidonians, and Hittites.

They were
from the nations that the Lord had warned the Israelites, “You must not intermarry with them, for they will undoubtedly convince you to worship their gods.” Yet Solomon because of his love for women held on to them.

He had
seven hundred wives of noble birth and three hundred concubines. His wives did convince him to turn away from the Lord.

As Solomon
grew old, his wives led him to follow other gods, and he did not commit himself wholeheartedly to the Lord as his father David had done.

Solomon worshiped
Ashtoreth, goddess of the Sidonians, and Molech, the vile god of the Ammonites.

This was
how Solomon did evil in the Lord's sight, and was not completely dedicated to the Lord as his father David was.

It was
then that Solomon built a high place of worship for Chemosh, the vile god of the people of Moab, and for Molech, the vile god of the Ammonites, on a hill east of Jerusalem.

He built
places of worship for all his foreign wives where they burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.

The Lord
became angry with Solomon because he had turned away from the Lord, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice.

The Lord
had warned Solomon about this—that he should not worship other gods. But Solomon did not listen to the Lord's warning.

So the
Lord told him, “Since this is what you have done, and since you have not kept my agreement and my laws that I commanded, I will definitely take the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant.

However, for
the sake of your father David, I will not do this in your lifetime—I will take it away from your son.

Even then
I will not take away the whole kingdom. I will leave your son with one tribe for the sake of my servant David, and for the sake of my chosen city Jerusalem.”

Then the
Lord encouraged Hadad the Edomite of Edom's royal family to oppose Solomon.

Previously, when
David was in Edom, Joab the commander of the Israelite army had gone to bury some of his soldiers who had been killed, and had slaughtered every male in Edom.

Joab and
the whole Israelite army had spent six months there destroying them all.

But Hadad
and some Edomites who had been his father's officials had run away to Egypt—Hadad was just a boy at the time.

They left
Midian and went to Paran. Then, along with some people from Paran, they went to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt. He provided Hadad with a house and food, and also assigned him land as a gift.

Pharaoh became
very friendly with Hadad, and he gave him the sister of his own wife to marry, Queen Tahpenes' sister.

She gave
birth to his son called Genubath. Tahpenes brought him up in Pharaoh's palace with Pharaoh's own children.

However, when
news reached Hadad in Egypt that both David and Joab, the commander of the army, had died, Hadad said to Pharaoh, “Let me leave and return to my own country.”

Pharaoh asked
him, “Is there anything that you have lacked here with me that now you want to go back to your own country?”“No, there's nothing,” Hadad replied, “but please just let me go home.”

God also
encouraged Rezon, son of Eliada, to oppose Solomon. He had run away from his master Hadadezer, king of Zobah. After David had destroyed Zobah's army,

Rezon gathered
around him a rebel band, and became their leader. They went and settled in Damascus, where they took over.

Rezon was
Israel's enemy throughout Solomon's lifetime which added to the trouble Hadad caused. Rezon really hated Israel, and was the ruler of Aram.
chapter.heading: Adversaries Arise
chapter.v:
In addition,
Jeroboam, son of Nebat, rebelled against the king. One of Solomon's officials, he was an Ephraimite from Zeredah. His mother was a widow called Zeruah.

This is
why he rebelled against the king: Solomon had built the terraces and had closed the gap in the wall of the city of his father David.

Jeroboam was
a man of ability, and when Solomon realized how successful he was in what he did, he placed him in command of all the forced labor of the tribes of Joseph.

Around that
time the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met Jeroboam on the road as he was leaving Jerusalem.

Ahijah had
wrapped himself in a new cloak, and the two of them were by themselves in the countryside. Ahijah took the new cloak he was wearing and ripped it up into twelve pieces.

He said,
“Jeroboam, take ten pieces. This is what the Lord God of Israel says. ‘Jeroboam, I am the Lord, the God of Israel, and I am going to take Solomon's kingdom from him and give you ten of the tribes.

One tribe
will be left for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I chose from among all the tribes of Israel.

This is
because they have abandoned me and bowed down in worship of Ashtoreth, goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh, god of the Moabites, and Molech, god of the Ammonites. They have not followed my ways; they have not done what is right in my sight; they have not kept my commandments and laws as David, Solomon's father, did.

Even so,
I'm not going to take the whole kingdom from Solomon, because I made him ruler for his lifetime for the sake of my servant David. I chose him because he kept my commandments and laws.

But I
will take from his son's kingdom ten tribes and give them to you.

I will
give his son one tribe, so that my servant David will always have a descendant like a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city where I chose to be honored.

I will
take you, and you shall reign over everything that you want. You will be king over Israel.

If you
accept everything that I command you, if you follow my ways, if you do what is right in my sight, keeping my laws and commandments as my servant David did, then I will be with you. I will set up for you a dynasty that lasts, just as I did for David, and I will give Israel to you.

I will
punish David's descendants because of this, but not forever.’”

So Solomon
tried to kill Jeroboam. But Jeroboam ran away to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt. He remained there until Solomon's death.

The record
of the rest of the acts of Solomon, including everything he did, and his wisdom, are written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon.

Solomon reigned
in Jerusalem over all of Israel for a total of forty years.

Solomon died
and was buried in the city of his father David. His son Rehoboam succeeded him as king.
